paras: The attempted burning of the Richardson house in Clive, Iowa, was an arson attempt in about early August 1903 on the house where Chas. Richardson had lived and where his son Elmer still lived, in a village five miles west of Des Moines. Neighbors put out the fire, and no one was hurt. The Iowa State Bystander reported it as the first of a series of attacks that it attributed to "White Caps" seeking to drive colored residents from Clive.

According to the Bystander, Clive's colored residents numbered fewer than a dozen families, who owned their homes and some valuable land. Chas. Richardson had moved to town, leaving his son Elmer living alone in the house.

About two weeks before the dynamiting of I. J. Anderson's house, someone soaked the door of the Richardson house with coal oil and set it alight while Elmer Richardson was away. Neighbors saw the blaze and put it out.

The campaign continued around Aug. 22, when dynamite placed under Anderson's house shattered the chimney and part of the walls, and a card was posted declaring "All negroes are warned to 'git'" and threatening white employers. Unsigned letters warned Ex-Representative Chas. Steward, the Milwaukee section boss Mr. Olesen and a Mr. Kirk not to hire colored people.
The Bystander reported that "the better element of whites" were indignant and were working with the colored residents to find those responsible. No report of an arrest appears in the coverage.

White papers learned of the Clive attacks through a Des Moines wire of Aug. 24-26, run under headlines such as "Warn Negroes to Leave" and "Negroes in Terror" in New York, Illinois and North Dakota. The wire centered on the notices and the Anderson dynamiting and ended with one sentence saying an effort had been made two weeks earlier to burn Anderson's home, without naming the Richardsons. Vermont weekly digests shrank the story to a single line, "Clive, Io., whitecaps warn negroes to leave town."

The Iowa State Bystander, a Des Moines Black weekly, gave the only account naming the Richardson house, under the headline "Clive Iowa the Scene of White Caps." In an editorial in the same issue, its editor, who had interviewed residents, called the attackers "cowardly villains," warned that "white capism" and lynching were "fast speeding to the north," and said they should be imprisoned for life or hanged if caught.

The Bystander placed the earlier fire at the Richardson house, while the wire attributed a burning attempt at the same interval to Anderson's own home. The two papers also differed on the size of the colored community, the wire giving "several hundred" against the Bystander's "less than a dozen families."

reader.title: Attempted burning of the Richardson house in Clive, Iowa
bases: The Bystander reports an attempt to set fire to the house with coal oil on the door, with no one hurt and no one present (A4); the wires report a burning attempt at the same interval (A1, A2).

Only the Bystander places the fire at the Richardson house (A4); the Des Moines wire reports a burning attempt about two weeks before the dynamiting but at Isaac Anderson's home (A1, A2, A3), which may be the same fire attributed to a different house.

accounts.label: Des Moines wire
accounts.gist: Supposed whitecaps posted notices ordering Clive's colored residents to leave, dynamited Isaac Anderson's house, and two weeks earlier had tried to burn his home.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Warn Negroes to Leave' and 'Negroes in Terror' center the notices and the Anderson dynamiting; the burning attempt is a single closing sentence about Anderson's home.
News digests reduced the affair to one line, 'Clive, Io., whitecaps warn negroes to leave town', with no mention of fire.
The Bystander called the attackers 'cowardly villains' and a 'monster of prejudice and hate', warned that 'white capism' and lynching were spreading north, and urged life terms or hanging.
